prompt: BEL (19.95%) and HAL (19.67%) both sit just under 20% in the Nifty India Defence index, while some websites show HAL above 26%. What best explains the gap?
options: The websites are using a different, uncapped market-cap calculation; the official index caps each stock at 20% at rebalancing, and weights then drift with prices until the next rebalance.
HAL's shares were sold by the government last week.
Index weights are decided by fund managers each month.
The official factsheet has an error.
why: Nifty India Defence weights are free-float market cap, capped at 20% per stock when the index is rebalanced. Between rebalances, weights move with share prices. Third-party sites often show raw market-cap shares without the cap, so their numbers differ.
wrong: Nothing in the data suggests a stake sale; the difference is method, not an event.
Index weights follow rules, not anyone's judgement — that's what makes an index passive.
The factsheet is the official source; other numbers are calculated differently.
big: Caps exist so one or two stocks can't dominate a theme index. Even so, BEL and HAL together are almost 40% of the defence index — the theme is concentrated.
client: "Almost 40% of a defence index fund is just two companies — BEL and HAL. You're buying a theme, but mostly those two."
remember: Always use the official factsheet; capped and uncapped weights are different numbers.

prompt: Between two factsheets, a stock's index weight rose from 5.6% to 6.6%, but no rebalancing happened. What is the most likely reason?
options: Its share price rose more than the index's other stocks, so its share of the index's total value increased.
The AMC bought more of it.
SEBI raised its weight.
Its dividend was cut.
why: Between rebalances, weights change mainly because of relative price movement. If one stock outperforms the rest, its slice of the index grows automatically.
wrong: Index funds follow the index; they don't decide weights.
SEBI doesn't set index weights; NSE Indices applies its methodology.
A dividend cut doesn't directly change free-float market cap weighting.
big: Rising weights often mean recent outperformance — not a signal about future returns. A stock that has run up becomes a bigger part of the index right when it may be more expensive.
client: "Its weight went up because its price went up faster than the others — that's a result of past performance, not a prediction."
remember: Weight up between rebalances = price up relative to peers.

prompt: Nifty India Defence trades at a P/E of about 58 while Nifty Metal trades at about 17 (30 Sep 2026). A client asks which is 'better value'. What's the most responsible answer?
options: Metal, because a lower P/E always means a better investment.
Defence, because a high P/E shows the strongest companies.

The P/E shows how much investors are paying for each rupee of current earnings. Defence's high P/E reflects strong growth expectations — which also means more disappointment risk. Metal's low P/E reflects cyclical earnings that can fall. Neither number alone tells you which suits you.
P/E ratios don't matter for index funds.
why: P/E compares price to earnings. A high P/E means investors expect strong future growth; a low P/E can mean cheap — or that earnings are expected to fall. Context matters.
wrong: Cyclical sectors like metals often look cheapest at their earnings peak.
High P/E reflects expectations, not quality, and raises the bar for future results.
Index valuations matter because the fund owns those same companies at those prices.
big: Defence's 5-year price CAGR of about 50% helped push its valuation up. Strong past returns plus high valuations is exactly when thematic sizing matters most.
client: "Defence investors are paying for a lot of future growth already. That's fine in a small slice, but it means falls can be sharp if growth disappoints."
remember: High P/E = high expectations, not high quality.

prompt: In the Nifty India Defence factsheet, 13.27% of the index is 'Automobile & Auto Components' and 11.90% is 'Chemicals'. What explains this?
options: Bharat Forge (a forging/auto-components company with a defence business) and Solar Industries (explosives, classified as chemicals) are large constituents.
The index includes car makers by mistake.
SEBI requires every index to hold three sectors.
These are cash holdings.
why: Companies are included if they meet the defence criteria (eligible industry, or at least 10% revenue from defence), but the factsheet classifies them by their main industry. Bharat Forge exactly equals the 13.27% auto component weight; Solar Industries equals the 11.90% chemicals weight.
wrong: Eligibility rules explicitly allow companies with meaningful defence revenue from other industries.
There's no such rule.
Index weights are stocks, not cash.
big: Reading sector weights tells you what you really own: a defence index is also partly an auto-component and explosives bet.
client: "About a quarter of this defence index comes from companies whose main business is forgings or explosives — read the factsheet, not just the name."
remember: Theme names hide sector mixes — check the factsheet.

prompt: The Nifty India Defence index had 19 constituents on 31 Aug 2026 and 22 on 30 Sep 2026. What does this most likely reflect?
options: The semi-annual reconstitution added stocks that met the eligibility rules.
Three companies merged.
The index fund manager chose new stocks.
Defence companies split their shares.
why: The index is reconstituted semi-annually with the broad Nifty indices. New listings or companies meeting the size and defence-revenue rules can be added at that time.
wrong: A merger would reduce, not increase, the count.
Index funds follow the index; they don't pick stocks.
Share splits don't change the number of constituents.
big: More constituents can mean more small, volatile companies in the tail — the top two stocks still dominate.
client: "The index added companies at its regular review — the big names still drive most of the movement."
remember: Constituent changes happen at scheduled reviews, by rule.

prompt: Nifty Metal's 1-year price return was about +27% while Nifty IT's was about −18% (to 30 Sep 2026). A client wants to move his IT fund into a metal fund. What's the key point to explain?
options: Metal sectors are cyclical; profits swing with global commodity prices and demand, so last year's leader can reverse. Switching sectors on one year's return is performance chasing.
Metals always outperform IT.
IT companies are shutting down.
Metal funds have no risk.
why: Sector leadership rotates. Metals benefit when commodity prices and industrial demand rise, and suffer when they fall. IT depends on global technology spending and the rupee. A one-year gap says little about the next year.
wrong: Long-term data shows leadership changing; IT outperformed in many earlier years.
A weak year for share prices isn't business failure.
Metal indices have high volatility — the factsheet standard deviation is above 25%.
big: Sector funds should be sized as satellites. Switching between them adds tax and timing risk.
client: "Metals had a strong year and IT a weak one. Next year could be different — that's why we don't build a plan around one sector."

prompt: Hindustan Zinc is in Nifty Metal. Why might silver prices matter for it?
options: It produces silver as a by-product of zinc and lead mining, so silver prices affect its earnings.
It owns silver ETFs.
SEBI links its weight to silver prices.
It doesn't — zinc companies never produce silver.
why: Most of the world's silver comes as a by-product of mining other metals like zinc, lead and copper. Hindustan Zinc is a significant silver producer for this reason.
wrong: It's a miner, not an investor in ETFs.
Index weights follow free-float market cap.
By-product silver is common and significant.
big: This links two lessons: silver supply is slow to respond to price because most of it is a by-product.
client: "Some metal companies earn from several metals at once — Hindustan Zinc is a zinc and silver story."
remember: Silver often comes out of zinc mines.

prompt: In Nifty IT, Infosys's weight rose from 29.17% (30 Sep 2025) to 31.30% (30 Sep 2026), and Coforge's from 5.62% to 6.59%. What's the most reasonable reading?
options: Both stocks did better than the rest of the index over the year (and/or gained at rebalancing), so their share of the index increased.
Infosys and Coforge merged.
The index added more Infosys shares on request of investors.
Their weights rose because the index return was negative.
why: Weights reflect relative free-float market value. When some constituents fall less (or rise more) than others, their weights rise — even in a falling index, as Nifty IT was down about 18% over the year.
wrong: No merger occurred.
Investors don't influence index weights.
A falling index doesn't by itself raise any particular stock's weight.
big: Mid-sized IT firms like Coforge and Persistent have been gaining weight versus the largest names — a shift within the sector.
client: "Within IT, some companies have held up better than others — the index weights show that shift."
remember: Weights show relative performance inside a sector.

prompt: Why do Nifty IT companies tend to benefit when the rupee weakens?
options: Most of their revenue is earned in foreign currencies (mainly from North America and Europe) while many costs are in rupees.
The RBI pays them a subsidy.
A weak rupee makes their software free.
They import all their raw materials.
why: Indian IT firms earn the large majority of revenue overseas. When the rupee weakens, those dollar or euro revenues convert into more rupees, which can support margins.
wrong: There's no such subsidy.
Currency doesn't change pricing in that way.
IT services companies don't depend on imported raw materials.
big: This makes IT a partial natural hedge in portfolios when the rupee is under pressure — though demand from global clients matters more over time.
client: "IT companies earn in dollars, so a weaker rupee can help them — but what really drives them is global tech spending."

prompt: The largest sector in Nifty Infrastructure (30 Sep 2026) is Oil, Gas & Consumable Fuels at 27.42%, with Reliance alone at 19.86%. What should an RM take from this?
options: An index's name doesn't fully describe its exposure; an 'infrastructure' fund here is heavily tied to Reliance and energy, so check the factsheet before recommending it.
The index is wrongly constructed.
Infrastructure funds hold no construction companies.
Oil companies are always infrastructure.
why: The index includes telecom, power, ports and similar businesses, and Reliance qualifies with a large free-float value. It is capped at 20%, which is why it sits just under that limit.
wrong: It follows its published rules.
L&T (construction) is about 12%.
Classification is specific to this index's rules.
big: Many clients already own Reliance, Airtel and L&T through large-cap funds — adding an infra index fund may increase overlap.
client: "This 'infrastructure' index is about a fifth Reliance. You may already own a lot of it through your other funds."
remember: Read the factsheet, not the fund name.
